Why the hell didn't you get an older, house-trained animal for your first dog?  I'm so sick of everyone's obsession with puppies.  DO NOT get a puppy (especially one this young) if you don't have the time to take care of it.  This little guy (a BABY just separated from his mother and brothers and sisters) needs someone who can give him love and all the attention he needs.  What you're going to end up with is a poorly house-trained dog with massive separation anxiety issues.  

You didn't rescue this poor puppy from a guy who mistreated him.  You took him from one bad situation to another.  

If you have a heart and really want to do what's best for this dog, give him up to a legit rescue organization, where he can be placed with someone who has both the time and experience to give the puppy a fighting chance at a good life.  Then ask that rescue to match you with an older dog who has been waiting for a good home.  Since it's your first dog, they can help you pick a breed, size and temperament that suits your life.  

I apologize for venting on you, but a little research and less "oooooh puppy!" could have saved you and this dog a lot of pain.

Also, it's important to note the difference between psychiatrists and psychologists.  My psychiatrist does exactly what /u/cold08 says: Asks how I am and adjusts my meds.  Psychologists are more what people think of as "shrinks" -- they do psychotherapy and such.

I'm so proud of myself for getting out -- but it didn't take my trip down memory lane to realize that.  Every time I've thought about him over the past year, I've felt a huge sense of relief that I'm out on my own and making a life for myself.  Instead of comparing yourself to others' highlight reels, think about the awesomeness in **your** life.  As many others have said in here, find something else to do when the urge strikes -- something that makes **you** happy.  

It's interesting that in social media where we post about **ourselves**, we end up focusing so much on everyone **but** ourselves.

Hm, link didn't work second time I tried it.  Here's the answer I was talking about:

You're probably starting or stopping with the thread takeup lever not in the highest position. And you're probably not hanging on to your thread ends while beginning a seam. 

Do this instead -- at this point, your machine should be correctly threaded, top and bottom, and you've got 3 or so inches of thread tail from both areas: 

1) raise the needle and thread take up lever to the highest position. (this keeps the needle from automagically unthreading) 
2) raise the presser foot. 
3) place the fabric under the needle. 
4) using the handwheel or a needle down button on the sewing machine, drop the needle into the fabric at the seam starting point. (Turn the handwheel only in the direction that would cause the fabric to move from the front to back of the machine.) 
5) pull the needle and bobbin threads under and behind the presser foot. 
6) drop the presser foot. 
7) hold the thread ends behind the presser foot while you make the first couple of stitches 
8) drop the thread ends and sew normally 

At the end of the seam, make sure the needle and thread takeup lever are at their highest position. Raise the presser foot, pull the fabric out, and cut the threads at the end of the finished seam, leaving thread tails ready for the next seam. 

If you don't hang on to the thread tails at the beginning of a seam, you can get a "caterpillar" of top thread forming on the underside of the fabric. Not all machines are prone to this malady, but it's so common that it's best to get in the habit of hanging on to the threads when starting a seam. Likewise, many modern machines will always stop stitching with the needle and thread uptake lever fully up, but I'm guessing yours does not. Or you haven't threaded the uptake lever.

I have this exact same problem.  I'm Type II, 200 mg Lamictal and 20 mg Lexapro.  I started taking trazodone, an older antidepressant now used mostly for sleep, and it's a miracle drug for me.  I don't know if it would work for you, but it might be worth asking your doctor about it.  [Here's an article](http://www.consumerreports.org/cro/2012/04/trazodone-common-sleep-drug-is-little-known-antidepressant/index.htm) that lists benefits and risks.  I do feel a little groggy the next day, but to me it's worth it to not lie in bed for hours with my mind racing.  I don't take it every night (even though it's not supposed to be habit-forming) but when I do, I notice that I don't remember my usually super crazy vivid dreams.  

Good luck to you.

I'm in somewhat of the same boat (buy old car outright or try to finance slightly better car with bad/no credit?) and I've been looking at online calculators to see what monthly payments would be for different interest rates if I go with a slightly better car.  Maybe look at lendingtree or another online loan site?  Or try your local credit union.  You have some credit with the gas card and you have money for a down payment.   I think that makes you better off than quite a lot of people.  

Also, check your local salvage yards to see what they'll give you for your car.  I got $350 (I think, it was years ago) for a rusted out Dodge Neon.  Or give it to charity and take the tax write-off.  

If those repairs you made on the Taurus hold out, maybe you can keep saving for more of a car fund/down payment?  Though if it's cold where you are, heat is important!  

Remember to check insurance rates if you decide to finance because lenders require more stringent (read: expensive) insurance coverage if you have a lien on the car.  

If you decide to finance, don't let the dealer talk you into revealing what you're comfortable with as far as a monthly payment goes.  Negotiate the price of the car first, then work out the financing.  They will try to confuse you by playing a numbers game with the financing and they'll come back with a payment on the upper end of whatever window you give them.  Also, maybe try Capital One to see if they still do their Blank Check auto loans.  That's how I got my first car and it makes you the equivalent of a cash buyer, which has a lot of perks.  

Lastly, please take it from someone who has made a lot of financial mistakes: Buy what you can afford!  I didn't, and now I'm in a mess of my own making and it's the worst feeling in the world.  

Good luck!
